info.bio: Herbert "Herb" Alpert (Los Ángeles (California, EEUU), 31 de marzo de 1935) es un trompetista y cantante estadounidense conocido por formar parte del grupo Herb Alpert and The Tijuana Brass, Herb Alpert's Tijuana Brass o simplemente TJB. También es famoso por ser un ejecutivo de la industria de grabación - él es la letra "A" de A & M Records (un sello de grabación fundado junto a Jerry Moss). Los logros musicales de Alpert son de cinco números uno

scenes.name: El pop de papá y mamá
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los adultos compraban LPs (a 32 chelines frente a los 6 de un single) y también muchos singles, de modo que la lista británica de 1965 era esquizofrénica: los Stones y los Beatles competían con lo que los adolescentes llamaban «música de papás y mamás», Ken Dodd, los Seekers, los Bachelors o Jim Reeves. La banda sonora de The Sound of Music encabezó la lista de LPs casi todo 1965 y 1966. Los adolescentes más jóvenes encontraban nuevos ídolos como los Walker Brothers, baladistas melodramáticos a lo Spector.

scenes.name: Bad Boy, Biggie y los Hitmen
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Christopher Wallace, hijo de una jamaicana que trabajaba en dos empleos para pagarle el colegio, era Peter Parker en casa y Spider-Man en la esquina; dejó los estudios por el trapicheo, pasó nueve meses en la cárcel y su maqueta con 50 Grand llegó a Mister Cee y a la columna Unsigned Hype de Matty C: «el segundo advenimiento de Kane con la voz de KRS». Sean «Puff Daddy» Combs, bailarín de Heavy D y becario de Uptown con Andre Harrell, había inventado el hip-hop soul (las mezclas de R&B y breaks para Jodeci y Mary J. Blige); despedido en 1993, se quedó a Biggie y fundó Bad Boy con Arista, y lo sacó de Carolina del Norte horas antes de una redada. Como Belichick y Brady, la tensión los hacía mejores: Biggie no escribía nada; Puff le pedía éxitos sobre hits de los ochenta («Juicy» sobre Mtume, «Big Poppa» sobre los Isley) para vender a las mujeres sin perder la dureza. Ready to Die (septiembre de 1994) rompió el dominio del Oeste; antes «Flava in Ya Ear» de Craig Mack había abierto camino. Biggie colocó a Junior M.A.F.I.A. y a Lil’ Kim; Mary J. Blige, reina del hip-hop soul, le trajo a The Lox. Los Hitmen (D-Dot, Nashiem Myrick, Carlos Broady, Stevie J, Chucky Thompson…), en parejas que competían, samplearon soul de Memphis y en Trinidad grabaron No Way Out y Life After Death. Biggie murió tiroteado en Los Ángeles el 9 de marzo de 1997, con veinticuatro años; el doble disco salió dos semanas después. Su sueño de convertir la cultura en negocio lo cumplió Jay-Z.

podcast.title: Connection to "Never Say Never Again" Theme (1983)
podcast.body: Herb Alpert, co-founder of A&M Records, is connected to the "Never Say Never Again" theme through his marriage to Lani Hall, who sang the song. This familial tie links a major record label figure to one of the less-remembered Bond themes. "She was married to her Belpert, the A and A and M records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Encounter with Gino Vannelli
podcast.body: Herb Alpert, at A&M Records, was directly approached by Gino Vannelli, who audaciously bypassed security to plead for a chance in music. Alpert responded by giving Vannelli the opportunity he sought. "Herb Alpert turned around and said, hey, okay, what is it? And he said, just give me a chance. And he did. Herb Alpert gave Gina Vannelly the chance that he was looking for."

xref.title: Second Custom Concert Sound System (1965)
xref.body: In 1965, Herb Alpert and the Tijuana Brass contracted Harry McHughan sound systems for their tour. This initiative is noted as establishing what appears to be the second dedicated concert sound system for touring artists, following The Beach Boys' earlier efforts. "Then, Herb Alpert and the Tijuana Brass contracted Harry McHughan sound systems for their 1965 tour."

xref.title: A&M Records Signing and Antics
xref.body: Captain Beefheart and His Magic Band signed with A&M Records in 1966, an indie label co-founded by Herb Alpert. The label was notably indulgent of Beefheart over the years, despite his unpredictable behavior. One anecdote describes him showing up at the label's offices with a loaded crossbow, angered by criticism of his work. "Beefheart and his magic band were eventually signed to An M in 1966 and over the years the label indulged him a lot, even though he would do things like show up with a loaded crossbow at the offices because he was angry that somebody dared critique his work."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Commissioned Sound System
xref.body: The Beach Boys, along with Herb Alpert and the Tijuana Brass, commissioned a specially built sound system for their tours. This move reflected the growing demand for more powerful and effective concert amplification beyond standard PA systems, following issues faced by bands like The Beatles with inadequate volume for large crowds. "The Beach Boys commissioned a specially built sound system for their tours, so did her bellbird and the Tijuana brass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Commissioned Sound System
xref.body: Herb Alpert and the Tijuana Brass, alongside The Beach Boys, commissioned a specialized sound system for their tours. This initiative was part of a broader trend among popular bands to address the limitations of existing amplification for live music performances in the mid-1960s. "The Beach Boys commissioned a specially built sound system for their tours, so did her bellbird and the Tijuana brass."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
